questions.stem: Sam, 20, is seen in a GP clinic after severe breathlessness towards the end of his first 20 km run. He is now well. He has no chest pain, palpitations, dizziness or syncope. Before you move on to the examination, which further question best screens for an inherited cardiac cause such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
options: Does anyone in your family have high cholesterol or take tablets for their heart?
Have you or anyone in your family ever had a clot in the legs or lungs?
Has anyone in your family died suddenly or unexpectedly at a young age?
Did you have asthma, eczema or bad hay fever when you were a child?
questions.why: Sudden unexplained death in a young relative is the key family history red flag for an inherited cardiomyopathy or channelopathy (for example HCM or long QT) in a young athlete with exertional symptoms. If present, he needs an ECG and cardiology review before he trains hard again.
notes: High cholesterol is a risk factor for coronary disease later in life (Sam's dad takes a statin). It does not screen for the inherited cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias that cause exertional events in young athletes.
This screens for venous thromboembolism, which is a separate dangerous differential, not for inherited heart disease.
This screens for atopy and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, which is a respiratory differential, not an inherited cardiac cause.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, returns to the GP 3 weeks later. He now gets cough and chest tightness for 10 to 15 minutes after most of his training runs, and it is spring. His resting spirometry last visit was normal, with no significant bronchodilator response. You suspect exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Give salbutamol 200 micrograms via spacer 15 minutes before each run and review
Refer for a bronchial provocation test such as a mannitol or exercise challenge
Start budesonide-formoterol 200/6 micrograms, one inhalation as needed
Repeat resting spirometry with bronchodilator response in 4 weeks
questions.why: Normal resting spirometry does not exclude EIB. The diagnosis is confirmed with an indirect bronchial provocation test (mannitol, exercise or eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea challenge) before committing him to inhaler treatment.
notes: This is treatment on suspicion, not confirmation. A symptomatic response to a reliever is non-specific, and the diagnosis would stay unproven.
This is a treatment, not a diagnostic test. Guidelines advise confirming variable airflow limitation objectively before labelling him with asthma.
Resting spirometry is often normal in EIB because the bronchoconstriction is triggered by exercise. Repeating it is unlikely to show anything and delays the diagnosis.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, a runner with spring hay fever, is referred for a mannitol challenge to look for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Inhaled dry-powder mannitol is used because it mimics the main trigger of bronchoconstriction during exercise. What is that mechanism?
options: Direct stimulation of muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation by pollen allergen inhaled throughout the run
Diaphragm fatigue reducing tidal volume at high minute ventilation
Airway water loss makes lining fluid hyperosmolar, releasing mast cell mediators
questions.why: Breathing large volumes of relatively dry air during exercise evaporates water from the airway surface. The lining fluid becomes hyperosmolar, and mast cells release leukotrienes, histamine and prostaglandins, which cause bronchoconstriction. Mannitol reproduces this osmotic stimulus.
notes: This is how methacholine works, as a direct challenge. Mannitol and exercise are indirect stimuli that act through mediator release.
Allergen exposure can worsen airway inflammation in atopic people, but the trigger in EIB is the osmotic effect of hyperventilation, not an allergen.
Respiratory muscle fatigue does not cause bronchoconstriction, and mannitol has no effect on the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Sam, 20, is tall and slim and became acutely breathless while running. The GP requests an erect PA chest X-ray to exclude a primary spontaneous pneumothorax, and the radiologist specifically comments that lung markings reach the chest wall at the apices. Where are the subpleural blebs that usually rupture to cause this condition typically located?
options: Lingula of the left upper lobe
Right middle lobe near the horizontal fissure
questions.why: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax usually comes from rupture of subpleural blebs at the lung apices. Tall, thin young men are thought to have greater mechanical stress at the apex. On an erect film, air also collects at the apex, so that is where a small pneumothorax is looked for first.
notes: The bases are not the usual site of blebs. Air in an erect patient also rises to the apex, so a basal pneumothorax is mainly seen on supine films (the deep sulcus sign).
The lingula is not the typical site of blebs in primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
The middle lobe is not the typical site, and the horizontal fissure is not a site of predilection for blebs.
